questions.q: Why are duplicate rows specifically dangerous in a report, not just untidy?
options: They silently inflate every total built on top of them — double-counted revenue, double-counted units, a confidently wrong dashboard
They cause Power BI to crash immediately
They only affect the visual appearance of a table, never any calculations
Duplicates are automatically removed by Power BI, so they're never actually a problem
questions.explain: A duplicate row means every sum, count, or average built on that data is quietly wrong — the danger isn't cosmetic, it's numerical.

options: Every row that is an exact repeat of an earlier row — the first occurrence itself is never flagged
Every row in the DataFrame, regardless of content
Only the very first occurrence of a repeated row
Rows that contain any missing values
questions.explain: duplicated() flags repeats after the first occurrence — the original row that later gets repeated is left as False.

options: Removes duplicate rows based on the entire row matching, keeping the first occurrence
Removes every row that has any missing value
Removes the first occurrence and keeps all repeats
Only works if you specify a subset of columns first
questions.explain: Without a subset argument, drop_duplicates() compares entire rows and keeps the first occurrence of each unique row, removing the rest.

questions.q: What does the subset parameter in drop_duplicates(subset=["Product"]) do?
options: Narrows the duplicate check to only the specified columns, rather than comparing the entire row
Deletes the specified columns from the DataFrame entirely
Only works with numeric columns, never text columns
Has no effect and is purely optional documentation
questions.explain: subset restricts what counts as 'duplicate' to specific columns — two rows can differ in every other column and still be treated as duplicates if their Product values match.

questions.q: If two rows share the same Product but have different Revenue values, does drop_duplicates(subset=["Product"]) treat them as duplicates?
options: Yes — subset narrows the comparison to only the listed column(s), so a Product match alone counts as a duplicate regardless of other differences
No — any difference in any column always prevents a duplicate match
Only if Revenue is also identical
subset has no effect on this comparison
questions.explain: Using subset means only the listed column(s) are compared — a shared Product value alone is enough to be flagged as a duplicate, even with differing Revenue.
